section.heading: 5.7 Applications to Differential Equations
section.paragraph: This section describes continuous analogues of the difference equations studied in Section 5.6. In many applied problems, several quantities are varying continuously in time, and they are related by a system of differential equations:

Here $$x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ are differentiable functions of $$t$$ , with derivatives $$x_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,x_{n}^{\prime}$$ , and the $$a_{ij}$$ are constants. The crucial feature of this system is that it is linear. To see this, write the system as a matrix differential equation
$$\textbf{x} ′ ( t ) = A \textbf{x} ( t )$$
where

$$\textbf{x} ( t ) = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ \vdots \\ x_{n} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} , \mathbf{x} ' ( t ) = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1}^{′} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ \vdots \\ x_{n}^{′} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} , \text{and} A = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & \hdots & a_{1 n} \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ a_{n 1} & \hdots & a_{n n} \end{bmatrix}$$
A solution of equation (1) is a vector-valued function that satisfies (1) for all $$t$$ in some interval of real numbers, such as $$t \geq 0$$ .

Equation (1) is linear because both differentiation of functions and multiplication of vectors by a matrix are linear transformations. Thus, if $$\textbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are solutions of $$\textbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ , then $$c\textbf{u} + d\textbf{v}$$ is also a solution, because
$$\left(\right. c \textbf{u} + d \textbf{v} \left.\right) ' & = c \textbf{u} ' + d \textbf{v} ′ & = c A \textbf{u} + d A \textbf{v} = A \left(\right. c \textbf{u} + d \textbf{v} \left.\right)$$

(Engineers call this property superposition of solutions.) Also, the identically zero function is a (trivial) solution of (1). In the terminology of Chapter 4, the set of all solutions of (1) is a subspace of the set of all continuous functions with values in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

Standard texts on differential equations show that there always exists what is called a fundamental set of solutions to (1). If $$A$$ is $$n \times n$$ , then there are $$n$$ linearly independent functions in a fundamental set, and each solution of (1) is a unique linear combination of these $$n$$ functions. That is, a fundamental set of solutions is a basis for the set of all solutions of (1), and the solution set is an $$n \text{-dimensional}$$ vector space of functions. If a vector $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ is specified, then the initial value problem is to construct the (unique) function $$\textbf{x}$$ such that $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ and $$\textbf{x}(0) = \textbf{x}_{0}$$ .
When $$A$$ is a diagonal matrix, the solutions of (1) can be produced by elementary calculus. For instance, consider

$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}^{′} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ x_{2}^{′} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & - 5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ x_{2} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix}$$
that is,
$$x '_{1}^{} \left(\right. t \left.\right) & & = & 3 x_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) & x_{2}^{'} ( \textit{t} ) & = & - 5 x_{2} \left(\right. t \left.\right)$$

The system (2) is said to be decoupled because each derivative of a function depends only on the function itself, not on some combination or “coupling” of both $$x_{1}(t)$$ and $$x_{2}(t)$$ . From calculus, the solutions of (3) are $$x_{1}(t) = c_{1}e^{3t}$$ and $$x_{2}(t) = c_{2}e^{- 5t}$$ , for any constants $$c_{1}$$ and $$c_{2}$$ . Each solution of equation (2) can be written in the form

$$\left[\right. x_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) x_{2} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \left]\right. = \left[\right. c_{1} e^{3 t} c_{1} e^{- 5 t} \left]\right. = c_{1} \left[\right. 1 0 \left]\right. e^{3 t} + c_{2} \left[\right. 0 1 \left]\right. e^{- 5 t}$$
This example suggests that for the general equation $$\textbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ , a solution might be a linear combination of functions of the form
$$\textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \textbf{v} e^{\lambda t}$$

for some scalar $$\text{λ}$$ and some fixed nonzero vector v. [If $$\textbf{v} = \textbf{0}$$ , the function $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ is identically zero and hence satisfies $$\textbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ .] Observe that

$$\mathbf{x} ′ \left(\right. t \left.\right) & = & \lambda \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t} & \text{By} \text{calculus} , \text{since} \mathbf{v} \text{is} \text{a} \text{constant} \text{vector} A \mathbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) & = & A \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t} & \text{Multiplying} \text{both} \text{sides} \text{of} ( 4 ) \text{by} A$$

Since $$e^{ \text{λ} t}$$ is never zero, $$\mathbf{x}\prime(t)$$ will equal $$A\textbf{x}(t)$$ if and only if $$\text{λ} \textbf{v} = A\textbf{v}$$ , that is, if and only if $$\text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ and v is a corresponding eigenvector. Thus each eigenvalue–eigenvector pair provides a solution (4) of $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ . Such solutions are sometimes called eigenfunctions of the differential equation. Eigenfunctions provide the key to solving systems of differential equations.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: The circuit in Figure 1 can be described by the differential equation

$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}^{′} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ x_{2}^{′} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - \left(\right. 1 / R_{1} + 1 / R_{2} \left.\right) / C_{1} & 1 / \left(\right. R_{2} C_{1} \left.\right) \\ 1 / \left(\right. R_{2} C_{2} \left.\right) & - 1 / \left(\right. R_{2} C_{2} \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ x_{2} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix}$$

image.alt: A circuit diagram consists of two resistors and two capacitors.

example.paragraph: where $$x_{1}(t)$$ and $$x_{2}(t)$$ are the voltages across the two capacitors at time $$t$$ . Suppose resistor $$R_{1}$$ is $$1$$ ohm, $$R_{2}$$ is $$2$$ ohms, capacitor $$C_{1}$$ is $$1$$ farad, and $$C_{2}$$ is $$\text{.5}$$ farad, and suppose there is an initial charge of $$5$$ volts on capacitor $$C_{1}$$ and $$4$$ volts on capacitor $$C_{2}$$ . Find formulas for $$x_{1}(t)$$ and $$x_{2}(t)$$ that describe how the voltages change over time.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Let $$A$$ denote the matrix displayed above, and let $$\textbf{x}(t) = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {x_{1}(t)} \\ {x_{2}(t)} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . For the data given, $$A = \begin{bmatrix} {- 1.5} & {.5} \\ 1 & {- 1} \end{bmatrix},$$ and $$\textbf{x}(0) = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The eigenvalues of $$A$$ are $$\text{λ} _{1} = - .5$$ and $$\text{λ} _{2} = - 2$$ , with corresponding eigenvectors
$$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \text{and} \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

The eigenfunctions $$\textbf{x}_{1}(t) = \textbf{v}_{1}e^{ \text{λ} _{1}t}$$ and $$\textbf{x}_{2}(t) = \textbf{v}_{2}e^{ \text{λ} _{2}t}$$ both satisfy $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ , and so does any linear combination of $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ . Set

$$\textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} e^{\lambda_{1} t} + c_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} e^{\lambda_{2} t} = c_{1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{- .5 t} + c_{2} \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t}$$

and note that $$\textbf{x}(0) = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2}$$ . Since $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ are obviously linearly independent and hence span $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , $$c_{1}$$ and $$c_{2}$$ can be found to make $$\textbf{x}(0)$$ equal to $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ . In fact, the equation

$$c_{1} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 2\end{matrix} \left]\right. & + & c_{2} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 1 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}5 \\ 4\end{matrix} \left]\right. \uparrow & & \uparrow & & \uparrow \mathbf{v}_{1} & & \mathbf{v}_{2} & & \mathbf{x}_{0}$$
leads easily to $$c_{1} = 3$$ and $$c_{2} = - 2$$ . Thus the desired solution of the differential equation $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ is
$$\textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{- .5 t} - 2 \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t}$$
or

$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ x_{2} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 e^{- .5 t} & + & 2 e^{- 2 t} \\ 6 e^{- .5 t} & - & 2 e^{- 2 t}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

Figure 2 shows the graph, or trajectory, of $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ , for $$t \geq 0$$ , along with trajectories for some other initial points. The trajectories of the two eigenfunctions $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ lie in the eigenspaces of $$A$$ .

The functions $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ both decay to zero as $$t\rightarrow \text{∞}$$ , but the values of $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ decay faster because its exponent is more negative. The entries in the corresponding eigenvector $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ show that the voltages across the capacitors will decay to zero as rapidly as possible if the initial voltages are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign.

image.alt: A graph shows the origin attracting two straight lines and several curves.

section.paragraph: In Figure 2, the origin is called an attractor, or sink, of the dynamical system because all trajectories are drawn into the origin. The direction of greatest attraction is along the trajectory of the eigenfunction $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ (along the line through $$\textbf{0}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2})$$ corresponding to the more negative eigenvalue, $$\text{λ} = - 2$$ . Trajectories that begin at points not on this line become asymptotic to the line through $$\textbf{0}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ because their components in the $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ direction decay so rapidly.

If the eigenvalues in Example 1 were positive instead of negative, the corresponding trajectories would be similar in shape, but the trajectories would be traversed away from the origin. In such a case, the origin is called a repeller, or source, of the dynamical system, and the direction of greatest repulsion is the line containing the trajectory of the eigenfunction corresponding to the more positive eigenvalue.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Suppose a particle is moving in a planar force field and its position vector $$\textbf{x}$$ satisfies $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ and $$\textbf{x}(0) = \textbf{x}_{0}$$ , where
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & - 5 \\ - 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{x}_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} 2.9 \\ 2.6 \end{bmatrix}$$
Solve this initial value problem for $$t \geq 0$$ , and sketch the trajectory of the particle.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The eigenvalues of $$A$$ turn out to be $$\text{λ} _{1} = 6$$ and $$\text{λ} _{2} = - 1$$ , with corresponding eigenvectors $$\textbf{v}_{1} = ( - 5,2)$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = (1,1)$$ . For any constants $$c_{1}$$ and $$c_{2}$$ , the function

$$\textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} e^{\lambda_{1} t} + c_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} e^{\lambda_{2} t} = c_{1} \begin{bmatrix} - 5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{6 t} + c_{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} e^{- t}$$
is a solution of $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ . We want $$c_{1}$$ and $$c_{2}$$ to satisfy $$\textbf{x}(0) = \textbf{x}_{0}$$ , that is,

$$c_{1} \begin{bmatrix} - 5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + c_{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2.9 \\ 2.6 \end{bmatrix} \text{or} \begin{bmatrix} - 5 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c_{1} \\ c_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2.9 \\ 2.6 \end{bmatrix}$$
Calculations show that $$c_{1} = - 3/70$$ and $$c_{2} = 188/70$$ , and so the desired function is
$$\textbf{x} ( t ) = \frac{- 3}{70} \begin{bmatrix} - 5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{6 t} + \frac{188}{70} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} e^{- t}$$
Trajectories of $$\textbf{x}$$ and other solutions are shown in Figure 3.
example.heading: Figure 3
example.paragraph: The origin as a saddle point.

image.alt: A graph shows the origin as a saddle point with two straight lines splitting into several curves moving away from the origin.

figure.caption: Figure 2 The origin as an attractor

section.paragraph: In Figure 3, the origin is called a saddle point of the dynamical system because some trajectories approach the origin at first and then change direction and move away from the origin. A saddle point arises whenever the matrix $$A$$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues. The direction of greatest repulsion is the line through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{0}$$ , corresponding to the positive eigenvalue. The direction of greatest attraction is the line through $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ and $$\textbf{0}$$ , corresponding to the negative eigenvalue.
section.heading: Decoupling a Dynamical System
section.paragraph: The following discussion shows that the method of Examples 1 and 2 produces a fundamental set of solutions for any dynamical system described by $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ when $$A$$ is $$n \times n$$ and has $$n$$ linearly independent eigenvectors, that is, when $$A$$ is diagonalizable. Suppose the eigenfunctions for $$A$$ are
$$\textbf{v}_{1} e^{\lambda_{1} t} , \ldots , \textbf{v}_{n} e^{\lambda_{n} t}$$

with $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ linearly independent eigenvectors. Let $$P = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} \textbf{v}_{1} & \cdots & \textbf{v}_{n} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and let $$D$$ be the diagonal matrix with entries $$\text{λ} _{1},\ldots, \text{λ} _{n}$$ , so that $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ . Now make a change of variable, defining a new function $$\textbf{y}$$ by

$$\textbf{y} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = P^{- 1} \textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \text{or} , \text{equivalently} , \textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = P \textbf{y} \left(\right. t \left.\right)$$

The equation $$\textbf{x}(t) = P\textbf{y}(t)$$ says that $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ is the coordinate vector of $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ relative to the eigenvector basis. Substitution of $$P\textbf{y}$$ for x in the equation $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ gives
$$\frac{d}{d t} ( P \textbf{y} ) = A ( P \textbf{y} ) = ( P D P^{- 1} ) P \textbf{y} = P D \textbf{y}$$
Since $$P$$ is a constant matrix, the left side of (5) is $$P\textbf{y}\prime$$ . Left-multiply both sides of (5) by $$P^{- 1}$$ and obtain $$\textbf{y}^{\prime} = D\textbf{y}$$ , or

$$\begin{bmatrix} y_{1}^{′} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ y_{2}^{′} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ \vdots \\ y_{n}^{′} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_{1} & 0 & \hdots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_{2} & & \vdots \\ \vdots & & \ddots & 0 \\ 0 & \hdots & 0 & \lambda_{n} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} y_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ y_{2} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ \vdots \\ y_{n} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix}$$

The change of variable from $$\textbf{x}$$ to $$\textbf{y}$$ has decoupled the system of differential equations, because the derivative of each scalar function $$y_{k}$$ depends only on $$y_{k}$$ . (Review the analogous change of variables in Section 5.6.) Since $$y_{1}^{\prime} = \text{λ} _{1}y_{1}$$ , we have $$y_{1}(t) = c_{1}e^{ \text{λ} _{1}t}$$ , with similar formulas for $$y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}.$$ Thus

$$\textbf{y} ( t ) = \begin{bmatrix} c_{1} e^{\lambda_{1} t} \\ \vdots \\ c_{n} e^{\lambda_{n} t} \end{bmatrix} , \text{where} \begin{bmatrix} c_{1} \\ \vdots \\ c_{n} \end{bmatrix} = \textbf{y} ( 0 ) = P^{- 1} \textbf{x} ( 0 ) = P^{- 1} \textbf{x}_{0}$$
To obtain the general solution $$\textbf{x}$$ of the original system, compute

$$\textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) & = P \textbf{y} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}\textbf{v}_{1} & \hdots & \textbf{v}_{n}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \textbf{y} \left(\right. t \left.\right) & = c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} e^{\lambda_{1} t} + \hdots + c_{n} \textbf{v}_{n} e^{\lambda_{n} t}$$
This is the eigenfunction expansion constructed as in Example 1.
section.heading: Complex Eigenvalues
section.paragraph: In the next example, a real matrix $$A$$ has a pair of complex eigenvalues $$\text{λ}$$ and $$\overset{‾}{ \text{λ} }$$ , with associated complex eigenvectors v and $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{v}}$$ . (Recall from Section 5.5 that for a real matrix, complex eigenvalues and associated eigenvectors come in conjugate pairs.) So two solutions of $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ are

$$\textbf{x}_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \textbf{v} e^{\lambda t} \text{and} \textbf{x}_{2} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \overset{\overline}{\textbf{v}} e^{\overset{\overline}{\lambda} t}$$

It can be shown that $$\textbf{x}_{2}(t) = \overset{‾}{\textbf{x}_{1}(t)}$$ by using a power series representation for the complex exponential function. Although the complex eigenfunctions $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ are convenient for some calculations (particularly in electrical engineering), real functions are more appropriate for many purposes. Fortunately, the real and imaginary parts of $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ are (real) solutions of $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ , because they are linear combinations of the solutions in (6):

$$\text{Re} ( \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t} ) = \frac{1}{2} [ \mathbf{x}_{1} ( t ) + \bar{\mathbf{x}_{1} ( t )} ] , \text{Im} ( \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t} ) = \frac{1}{2 i} [ \mathbf{x}_{1} ( t ) - \bar{\mathbf{x}_{1} ( t )} ]$$

To understand the nature of $$\text{Re} \left( \textbf{v}e^{ \text{λ} t} \right)$$ , recall from calculus that for any number $$x$$ , the exponential function $$e^{x}$$ can be computed from the power series:
This series can be used to define $$e^{ \text{λ} t}$$ when $$\text{λ}$$ is complex:
$$e^{\lambda t} = 1 + (\lambda t ) + \frac{1}{2 !} (\lambda t )^{2} + \hdots + \frac{1}{n !} (\lambda t )^{n} + \hdots$$
By writing $$\text{λ} = a + bi$$ (with $$a$$ and $$b$$ real), and using similar power series for the cosine and sine functions, one can show that
$$e^{\left(\right. a + b i \left.\right) t} = e^{a t} e^{i b t} = e^{a t} \left(\right. cos b t + i sin b t \left.\right)$$
Hence

$$\textbf{v} e^{\lambda t} & = \left(\right. \text{Re} \textbf{v} + i \text{Im} \textbf{v} \left.\right) \left(\right. e^{a t} \left.\right) \left(\right. cos b t + i sin b t \left.\right) & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}\left(\right. \text{Re} \textbf{v} \left.\right) cos b t - \left(\right. \text{Im} \textbf{v} \left.\right) sin b t\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} e^{a t} & + i \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}\left(\right. \text{Re} \textbf{v} \left.\right) sin b t + \left(\right. \text{Im} \textbf{v} \left.\right) cos b t\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} e^{a t}$$
So two real solutions of $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ are

$$\boxed{\textbf{y}_{1} ( t ) & = \text{Re} \textbf{x}_{1} ( t ) = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}\left(\right. \text{Re} \textbf{v} \left.\right) cos b t - \left(\right. \text{Im} \textbf{v} \left.\right) sin b t\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} e^{a t} \textbf{y}_{2} ( t ) & = \text{Im} \textbf{x}_{1} ( t ) = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}\left(\right. \text{Re} \textbf{v} \left.\right) sin b t + \left(\right. \text{Im} \textbf{v} \left.\right) cos b t\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} e^{a t}}$$
It can be shown that $$\textbf{y}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{y}_{2}$$ are linearly independent functions (when $$b \neq 0$$ ).1

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: The circuit in Figure 4 can be described by the equation

$$\begin{bmatrix} i_{L}^{′} \\ v_{C}^{′} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - R_{2} / L & - 1 / L \\ 1 / C & - 1 / \left(\right. R_{1} C \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_{L} \\ v_{C} \end{bmatrix}$$

image.alt: A circuit diagram consists of two resistors, one capacitor, and one inductor.

example.paragraph: where $$i_{L}$$ is the current passing through the inductor $$L$$ and $$v_{C}$$ is the voltage drop across the capacitor $$C$$ . Suppose $$R_{1}$$ is $$\text{5 ohms}$$ , $$R_{2}$$ is $$\text{.8 ohm}$$ , $$C$$ is $$.1$$ farad, and $$L$$ is $$.4$$ henry. Find formulas for $$i_{L}$$ and $$v_{C}$$ , if the initial current through the inductor is $$3$$ amperes and the initial voltage across the capacitor is $$3$$ volts.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: For the data given, $$A = \begin{bmatrix} {- 2} & {- 2.5} \\ 10 & {- 2} \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{x}_{0} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The method discussed in Section 5.5 produces the eigenvalue $$\text{λ} = - 2 + 5i$$ and the corresponding eigenvector $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} i \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The complex solutions of $$\textbf{x}^{\prime} = A\textbf{x}$$ are complex linear combinations of

$$\textbf{x}_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} i \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{\left(\right. - 2 + 5 i \left.\right) t} \text{and} \textbf{x}_{2} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} - i \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{\left(\right. - 2 - 5 i \left.\right) t}$$
Next, use equation (7) to write
$$\textbf{x}_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} i \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t} \left(\right. cos 5 t + i sin 5 t \left.\right)$$
The real and imaginary parts of $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ provide real solutions:

$$\textbf{y}_{1} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} - sin 5 t \\ 2 cos 5 t \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t} , \textbf{y}_{2} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \begin{bmatrix} cos 5 t \\ 2 sin 5 t \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t}$$

Since $$\textbf{y}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{y}_{2}$$ are linearly independent functions, they form a basis for the two-dimensional real vector space of solutions of $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ . Thus the general solution is
$$\textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = c_{1} \begin{bmatrix} - sin 5 t \\ 2 cos 5 t \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t} + c_{2} \begin{bmatrix} cos 5 t \\ 2 sin 5 t \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t}$$

To satisfy $$\textbf{x}(0) = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , we need $$c_{1}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack + c_{2}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , which leads to $$c_{1} = 1.5$$ and $$c_{2} = 3$$ . Thus
$$\textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = 1.5 \begin{bmatrix} - sin 5 t \\ 2 cos 5 t \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t} + 3 \begin{bmatrix} cos 5 t \\ 2 sin 5 t \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t}$$
or

$$\begin{bmatrix} i_{L} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \\ v_{C} \left(\right. t \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - 1.5 sin 5 t + 3 cos 5 t \\ 3 cos 5 t + 6 sin 5 t \end{bmatrix} e^{- 2 t}$$
See Figure 5.

image.alt: A graph shows a spiral point originating on the origin with various curves spiraling into four quadrants. A point at the end of one curve lying in the first quadrant is labeled x subscript 0.

figure.caption: Figure 5 The origin as a spiral point

section.paragraph: In Figure 5, the origin is called a spiral point of the dynamical system. The rotation is caused by the sine and cosine functions that arise from a complex eigenvalue. The trajectories spiral inward because the factor $$e^{- 2t}$$ tends to zero. Recall that $$- 2$$ is the real part of the eigenvalue in Example 3. When $$A$$ has a complex eigenvalue with positive real part, the trajectories spiral outward. If the real part of the eigenvalue is zero, the trajectories form ellipses around the origin.

note.title: Practice Problems
note.heading: Practice Problems
note.paragraph: A real $$3 \times 3$$ matrix $$A$$ has eigenvalues $$- .5$$ , $$.2 + .3i$$ , and $$.2 - .3i$$ , with corresponding eigenvectors

list.item: Is $$A$$ diagonalizable as $$A = PDP^{- 1}$$ , using complex matrices?
Write the general solution of $$\textbf{x}^{\prime} = A\textbf{x}$$ using complex eigenfunctions, and then find the general real solution.
Describe the shapes of typical trajectories.

section.paragraph: 1 Since $$\textbf{x}_{2}(t)$$ is the complex conjugate of $$\textbf{x}_{1}(t)$$ , the real and imaginary parts of $$\textbf{x}_{2}(t)$$ are $$\textbf{y}_{1}(t)$$ and $$- \textbf{y}_{2}(t)$$ , respectively. Thus one can use either $$\textbf{x}_{1}(t)$$ or $$\textbf{x}_{2}(t)$$ , but not both, to produce two real linearly independent solutions of $$\textbf{x}^{\prime} = A\textbf{x}$$ .
